newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo police chief to quit over shooting case.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo police chief to quit over shooting case.

text.p: Tokyo's police chief handed in his resignation on Thursday over an alleged cover-up of circumstances surrounding the shooting of the national police chief after last year's subway gassing.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference that Superintendant General Yukihiko Inoue, chief of the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department, would step down over his department's handling of the attempted assassination.
"Superintendent General Inoue handed in his resignation and necessary procedures are now under way," Kajiyama said.
Inoue's resignation would take effect on December 3, officials of the National Police Agency said.

For five months, Tokyo police investigators failed to report that one of their own officers had confessed to shooting national police chief Takaji Kunimatsu outside his Tokyo apartment building on March 30 last year.
Kunimatsu was shot four times from about 20 yards (metres) away by a masked man as he left the building. After spending three months in hospital he was able to resume his duties.

The officer who confessed told investigators he was a former member of the doomsday cult Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect), which is accused of the nerve gas attack on the Tokyo subway 10 days before the shooting.

Cult guru Shoko Asahara is on trial for the subway attack, in which 12 people died and thousands were harmed, and on 16 other charges ranging from kidnap-murders to illegal production of drugs and weapons.
The officer had been assigned to the headquarters of the investigation into the subway attack.
Japanese newspapers said they were tipped off about his confession by letters sent by an anonymous author, presumably one of the investigators, and accused Tokyo police of a cover-up.
The Tokyo police department said the officer who confessed was fired on Thursday but had not been arrested because of lack of evidence. He has not been identified.

Hundreds of frogmen and officers have failed to recover the gun the officer said he used in the shooting after a month dredging Tokyo's Kanda canal. He said he threw the weapon into the canal after the attack.
